items.followUp: Explain why evaporation cools the human body when sweat evaporates.

rubric.why: Identifies that evaporation can occur without the liquid reaching its boiling point.
rubric.description: States that evaporation occurs continuously, including below the boiling point.
rubric.how: Award for stating that evaporation occurs continuously or below the boiling point.

rubric.why: Identifies which molecules escape during evaporation.
rubric.description: Explains that higher-energy molecules at the liquid surface escape into the vapour.
rubric.how: Award for identifying high-energy surface molecules as those that escape.

rubric.why: Explains how evaporation lowers the temperature of the remaining liquid.
rubric.description: States that the average kinetic energy of the remaining molecules decreases, causing cooling.
rubric.how: Award for linking decreased kinetic energy of the remaining molecules to cooling.

rubric.why: Accounts for the energy used in evaporation and its cooling effect.
rubric.description: States that the energy for evaporation comes from the liquid or its surroundings, making evaporation a cooling process.
rubric.how: Award for stating that evaporation takes in energy from the liquid or surroundings and causes cooling.

modelAnswer: Evaporation occurs continuously from the surface of a liquid, even below its boiling point.
The higher-energy molecules at the surface escape into the vapour.
The average kinetic energy of the molecules left behind decreases, so the liquid becomes cooler.
The energy needed for evaporation is taken from the liquid and its surroundings; therefore, evaporation is a cooling process.

items.followUp: Calculate the mass of KOH needed to prepare 250 cm³ of a 0.20 M solution.

rubric.why: Checks the correct SI conversions of volume and concentration.
rubric.description: Converts the given volume to 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³ and concentration to 400 mol m⁻³.
rubric.how: Award for both correct SI conversions.

rubric.why: Checks use of concentration and volume to calculate the amount of NaOH.
rubric.description: Uses n = CV and obtains 0.20 mol of NaOH.
rubric.how: Award for the correct formula and amount in moles.

rubric.why: Checks the molar mass used for NaOH.
rubric.description: Gives the molar mass of NaOH as 0.040 kg mol⁻¹ (40 g mol⁻¹).
rubric.how: Award for the correct molar mass.

rubric.why: Checks the calculated mass of NaOH.
rubric.description: Gives the required mass as 0.008 kg, or 8 g.
rubric.how: Award for the correct final mass with a unit.

modelAnswer: Given: C = 0.4 mol dm⁻³ = 400 mol m⁻³; V = 500 cm³ = 5.00 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
Molar mass of NaOH = 23 + 16 + 1 = 40 g mol⁻¹ = 0.040 kg mol⁻¹.
Therefore, 0.008 kg (8 g) of NaOH is required.

items.followUp: Why do ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten but not when solid?

rubric.why: Identifies the forces that hold the ions together.
rubric.description: States that oppositely charged ions in an ionic lattice are held by strong electrostatic forces of attraction.
rubric.how: Award for identifying strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.

rubric.why: Connects the strong ionic attractions to the energy required for melting and boiling.
rubric.description: Explains that considerable energy is needed to overcome the attractions, resulting in high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award for linking the energy needed to overcome ionic attractions with high melting and boiling points.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds contain oppositely charged ions held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction in a lattice.
A considerable amount of energy is needed to overcome these forces, so ionic compounds have high melting and boiling points.

items.followUp: Write two features of the modern long-form periodic table.

rubric.why: Checks the basis on which elements are arranged in the long-form periodic table.
rubric.description: States that elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
rubric.how: Award for stating that atomic number increases across the arrangement.

rubric.why: Checks another valid structural or group feature of the table.
rubric.description: Gives a feature such as seven periods, eighteen groups, or similar valence-electron arrangements or chemical properties within a group.
rubric.how: Award for one correct structural feature or one correct feature of elements in the same group.

modelAnswer: Elements in the long-form periodic table are arranged in order of increasing atomic number.
The table has 7 horizontal periods and 18 vertical groups; elements in the same group have similar valence-electron arrangements and chemical properties.
